newsitem.title: UK: De Beers sees little Komdragmet fall-out on talks.
newsitem.headline: De Beers sees little Komdragmet fall-out on talks.

text.p: De Beers said it expected the reported shutdown of Komdragmet, the Russian diamond and precious metals sales agency, to have little impact on its talks to reach a crucial new diamond deal with Russia.
But a De Beers spokesman said it was yet unclear what effect the agency's closure might have on Russian leakages of rough gems onto world markets outside the terms of any sales pact.
He was reacting to a Financial Times report that Komdragmet has been closed and its responsibilities transferred to the Finance Ministry and the new Ministry of Industry.

None of which are, however, partners in negotiations with De Beers. De Beers already signed a memorandum of understanding with the Russian Ministry of Finance in February for a new diamond sales deal.
But a formal agreement has yet to be reached with Almazy Rossii-Sakha (ARS), which is Russia's largest diamond producer and the country's sole exporter.
"At this precise moment it is tricky to say what if any influence this closure will have (on negotiations with ARS), but probably not very much," a De Beers spokesman said.
Talks between De Beers and ARS will resume next week. Under the previous agreement, Russia had to sell 95 percent of its rough diamonds through De Beer's Central Selling Organisation.
Large amounts of gems were, however, sold outside that deal and many of these diamonds appeared to come from stockpiles controlled by Kondragmet.
But analysts said recent sales seem to come straight from the mines, making them confident the leaks will be plugged once De Beers and ARS reach a final agreement.
But the De Beers spokesman was less confident of this. "When it comes to leakages, it is difficult to say (what the impact might be)," he said.
He added De Beers was waiting to see how authority will be divided between the two Russian ministries.
But Michael Steel, market research director at precious metals refiner Johnson Matthey, said he expected no major changes in market conditions for palladium and platinum.
The FT report suggested that stockpile control would fall under the Finance Ministry, said Steel, adding that the Ministry used to exert a big influence on Kondragmet's sales.
"I don't think it (the agency's closure) is a fundamental change," he said.
About a quarter of world platinum and two thirds of palladium supply came from Russia last year. Both metals are used in car catalysts to filter exhaust fumes.
